title: Tasting, Comparing and Ranking Insect/Animal/Plant Protein for Muscle Building
summary: Follow-up to his bug-eating ethics video: he tastes and grades 10 protein sources (lentils, eggs, mushrooms, turkey, tofu, sardines, protein bar, crickets, whey, cricket powder) out of 20 on macros, micros, bioavailability, price, availability, shelf life and taste. Sardines win (17.5), eggs and whey tie at 16; insects score low mainly on price and availability. Conclusion: insect protein is nutritionally decent but overhyped and can never be a staple.
claims: His protein-source grading: macros 4, micros 4, bioavailability+digestibility 3, price 3, availability 1.5, shelf life 1.5, taste 3, total 20 points, all standardized to 100 g
Lentils per 100 g: 116 kcal, 9 g protein, 0.3 g fat, 20 g carbs; mainly a carb source with poorly bioavailable protein, anti-nutrients and flatulence for some
Lentils' real value is micronutrients: lots of fiber, potassium, iron, B6, selenium and manganese
Lentils are very cheap (under $1 per 100 g), keep 1.5 years dry and about a week cooked; total 13/20
He cooks lentils in an Instant Pot or crock pot and spices them afterwards, usually with Thai curry, because plain they are bland
Vegans looking for something beyond rice should eat lentils but must learn to cook them or they will tire of them quickly
Eggs give about 12 g protein and 10 g fat per 100 g; their protein is overrated and calories add up for people watching intake
About 90% of egg protein is bioavailable, one of the highest of any food
Lifters should eat the whole egg; eating only whites throws away the yolk where the vitamins and minerals are
Eggs are a micronutrient bomb: choline, vitamins D, A and E, some omega-3, calcium and iron, all highly bioavailable
Buy eggs from a farmer whose hens roam and eat insects; a deep orange yolk usually signals quality, very cheap supermarket eggs are garbage
Eggs keep 3-5 weeks but carry salmonella risk; plain they taste of little; total 16/20
Mushrooms have about 22 kcal and 3 g protein per 100 g, with poor protein bioavailability, especially raw
Mushrooms are rich in beta-glucan fiber and bioavailable vitamin D, so vegans should include them
Supermarket mushrooms are often poor quality and spoil within about a week; total 10.5/20
He cooks mushrooms in a pan with olive oil and soy sauce, marinating about 10 minutes so they stay juicy, then uses them as a sauce over rice or pasta
He now eats mostly turkey rather than chicken
Turkey is lean with good macros and about 80% protein bioavailability; meat from birds raised on antibiotics and poor feed digests worse
Turkey is rich in B3, B6, selenium, B12, phosphorus and zinc; costs about $3-5 per 100 g and keeps only 3-5 days in the fridge; total 14/20
People favor animal products because they taste good even without spices
Tofu per 100 g: 83 kcal, 10 g protein, 5 g fat, 1 g carbs, about 70% bioavailable when cooked; a low-calorie protein source but not dense
Tofu supplies calcium (often added in manufacturing), manganese, selenium, iron, zinc and magnesium, costs about $1 per 100 g, but tastes like nothing even when marinated; total 12/20
Canned sardines per 100 g: 200 kcal, 25 g protein, 11 g fat, 0 carbs, about 80% bioavailable; they can trigger gout
Sardines are dense in omega-3, iodine, calcium, B12 and iron
Buy real sea salt rather than table salt for iodine; fish is also a good iodine source
Plant foods scored well on micronutrients and can be eaten in large volume; a balanced diet picks foods for micros and uses animal products for bioavailable protein
He eats far more from the plant plate than the animal plate, but still relies on animal foods for protein bioavailability
Sardines keep about 5 years, are available worldwide and cheap; watch mercury; he eats them with mango chutney; top score 17.5/20, the sleeper pick
Protein bars per 100 g: 340 kcal, 14 g protein, 6 g fat, 65 g carbs; the calories are not justified and micros are low and often added; favor whole foods; total 12/20
Crickets per 100 g: 126 kcal, 13 g protein, 6 g fat, 5 g carbs; a balanced food, not just a protein source as the media claims
Cricket protein is about 90% bioavailable, but the chitin exoskeleton is hard to digest though not toxic; people allergic to shellfish may react
Crickets are high in calcium, iron, magnesium and bioavailable B12 that outranks some animal sources, plus vitamins A, C, D, E and K
Crickets cost about $15 per 100 g, a terrible deal compared with any other source because Western production is too low
Do not import insects from countries with weak oversight: parasite and pesticide risk; his supplier tests parasites below 2%
Roasted crickets taste good, nutty like sunflower seeds; avoid insect products doused in artificial flavors; total 11.5/20
Whey per 100 g: about 400 kcal, 86 g protein, 4 g fat, 1 g carb, 100% bioavailable, about $3 per 100 g, keeps about 2 years; total 16/20
Whey is a supplement to food intake; eat real food first
Cricket powder per 100 g: 445 kcal, 70 g protein, 18 g fat, 1 g carb
He claims you absorb about 20 g of whey vs 30 g of cricket powder per hour, and that an 80 g shake is only about 30% used because it transits in 1-1.5 h, so sip shakes slowly or take smaller ones
Protein matters only until you have enough to recover and build muscle; beyond that it is not the most important thing
Cricket powder costs $5 (Thailand) to $15 (US) per 100 g, tastes like crickets but more bitter, and may suit lactose-intolerant lifters; total 13.5/20
He eats a small packet of crickets as a snack about once a week and plans to try half cricket powder, half whey
Insects can never be a staple protein: too small, too costly, chitin; no culture used them as a main food; at most a snack or whey replacement
Think beyond protein: digestion, your relationship with food and its effects as you age matter more than size
A complete diet is doable with insects, vegan, or meat-based eating if you are intelligent about it
